item.title: Influenza A Virus as a Multivalent Active Particle: Statistical Mechanics of Binding, Motility, and Antiviral Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.09696v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this contribution, we review existing multivalent models of Influenza A Virus (IAV) systems to study virion dynamics and design of multivalent entry blockers. We review existing biochemical estimations of the dissociation constants and catalytic activities of the two virion ligands [hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA)], which can be used to develop quantitative theories and experiments. Multivalent models are statistical mechanics frameworks for studying the simultaneous interaction of multiple reversible ligand-receptor bonds. They quantify the effects of both combinatorial entropy terms and single-molecule ligand-receptor affinities. Multivalent frameworks led to the rationale of superselectivity, the ability of probes to sense specific concentrations of conjugated receptors. Multivalent models guided the design of antiviral nanomedicines constituted by polymeric scaffolds conjugated with small molecules such as sialic acid receptors targeting the ligands on the surface of the virion. Importantly, neuraminidase is an enzyme that limits the number of host-guest bonds through receptor desialylation. Like active particles, neuraminidase activity enhances virion motility in the extracellular medium. Modeling the dynamics of Influenza A virions requires developing out-of-equilibrium multivalent models.
item.dc:creator: Sumati Bhatia, Andreas Herrmann, Thomas Kolbe, Lalan Kumar, Daniel Lauster, Susanne Liese, Bortolo Matteo Mognetti

item.title: The effect of limb kinematics on the speed of a legged robot on granular media
item.description: arXiv:1303.7276v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving effective locomotion on diverse terrestrial substrates can require subtle changes of limb kinematics. Biologically inspired legged robots (physical models of organisms) have shown impressive mobility on hard ground but suffer performance loss on unconsolidated granular materials like sand. Because comprehensive limb-ground interaction models are lacking, optimal gaits on complex yielding terrain have been determined empirically. To develop predictive models for legged devices and to provide hypotheses for biological locomotors, we systematically study the performance of SandBot, a small legged robot, on granular media as a function of gait parameters. High performance occurs only in a small region of parameter space. A previously introduced kinematic model of the robot combined with a new anisotropic granular penetration force law predicts the speed. Performance on granular media is maximized when gait parameters minimize body acceleration and limb interference, and utilize solidification features of granular media.
item.dc:creator: Chen Li, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Haldun Komsuoglu, Daniel I. Goldman
